title: Simulation-Based Inference for an Epidemic Model
description: Rejection and SMC-ABC methods applied to an adaptive-network SIR model.
summary: How can we infer hidden epidemic parameters when the likelihood is difficult to evaluate?
context: This project studies an adaptive-network SIR model where individuals change their contacts as the epidemic evolves. The simulator produces realistic but complex observations without giving a convenient closed-form likelihood.
approach: I implemented a simulation-based workflow: generate candidate parameters, simulate epidemic trajectories, compare simulated and observed summaries, then progressively focus the search with Sequential Monte Carlo Approximate Bayesian Computation.
exploration: I explored the effect of summary statistics, distance thresholds, and particle populations on the inferred parameter distributions. The project made the trade-off between simulator fidelity and inference cost concrete.
takeaways: The main takeaway is a practical understanding of likelihood-free inference, calibration, and how modelling assumptions propagate into uncertainty.

title: Climate Time Series Forecasting
description: Trend and seasonality forecasting using the Solar Anywhere API.
summary: Can a compact forecasting workflow separate long-term climate trends from recurring seasonal structure?
context: The project uses weather and solar-irradiance time series collected through the Solar Anywhere API. The focus is on turning an external data source into a reproducible analysis rather than treating forecasting as a black box.
approach: I cleaned timestamps, inspected missingness, decomposed the series into trend and seasonal components, and compared forecasts across different horizons. Visual diagnostics were used alongside error metrics to understand when a model was reliable.
exploration: I explored how frequency, horizon, and seasonal assumptions change the forecast. The analysis also highlighted the importance of plotting residuals rather than relying on a single score.
takeaways: This work strengthened my time-series workflow: data validation first, a transparent baseline second, and model complexity only when it earns its place.
tools: Python, Pandas, Statsmodels, Matplotlib, Solar Anywhere API

title: INSEE Survey Analysis
description: Descriptive analysis of union-membership survey data.
summary: What can careful descriptive statistics reveal about patterns in survey responses?
context: This analysis uses union-membership data from an INSEE survey. The challenge is to describe categorical responses without hiding sampling limitations or turning associations into causal claims.
approach: I prepared the variables, checked distributions and missing values, built weighted descriptive summaries, and compared groups with clear tables and visualisations. Each result was written to keep the statistical question visible.
exploration: I explored how conclusions change across subgroups and how survey design affects interpretation. The project served as an exercise in communicating uncertainty and avoiding overclaiming.
takeaways: The key takeaway is that good survey analysis is as much about defining the population and limitations as it is about producing a chart.

title: Engine Failure Prediction
description: An unfinished machine-learning project exploring engine failure prediction.
summary: How can sensor data be used to identify early signs of engine failure?
context: This repository is an active work in progress. The goal is to investigate predictive signals in engine or equipment data while keeping the modelling pipeline explainable.
approach: The current work is focused on data inspection, feature preparation, and establishing reliable baseline models. Evaluation design and the final modelling approach are still being developed.
exploration: Future work includes improving validation, handling class imbalance, comparing feature strategies, and documenting model limitations before treating the results as reliable.
takeaways: This project is deliberately unfinished and should be read as an evolving experiment rather than a completed result.

title: CNN Face Recognition Model
description: An unfinished convolutional-neural-network project for face recognition.
summary: How can a CNN learn useful facial representations from a carefully prepared image dataset?
context: This repository is an active work in progress exploring image preprocessing, convolutional architectures, and face-recognition modelling.
approach: The current work is centred on preparing the dataset and building an initial CNN training workflow. Architecture choices, evaluation, and generalisation testing are not final.
exploration: Future work includes improving the dataset pipeline, tuning the architecture, checking performance on unseen identities, and documenting privacy and bias considerations.
takeaways: This project is clearly unfinished: results and implementation choices may change substantially as the experiment develops.
